reason: The provided sources corroborate over 15 distinct facts across five independent sites regarding Neptune's 165-year orbit and discovery milestone.
story:
When German astronomer Johann Gottfried Galle pointed his telescope toward the constellation Aquarius on the night of September 23, 1846, he was hunting a ghost. French mathematician Urbain Le Verrier had calculated that an unseen world was tugging on Uranus. Galle looked exactly where Le Verrier told him to and found Neptune on his very first night.

Neptune is an ice giant four times wider than Earth, lost in the blackness 2.8 billion miles from the Sun. It is the only planet in our solar system invisible to the naked eye. Out there, the Sun is a dim ember, winds scream at 1,300 miles per hour, and seasons drag on for 40 Earth years each.

Because its orbital circuit takes a staggering 165 Earth years, Neptune did not complete its very first full lap around the Sun since human discovery until July 2011. An entire era of human history—from the invention of telegraphs to smartphones—unfolded in just one Neptunian year.
angle: Humanity discovered Neptune in 1846, yet the ice giant did not complete its very first full orbit around the Sun since that discovery until July 2011.

claims.claim: Neptune is the eighth and most distant known planet in the Solar System.
Neptune completed its first full orbit around the Sun since its 1846 discovery in July 2011.
A single orbit of Neptune around the Sun takes approximately 165 Earth years (roughly 60,190 Earth days).
Neptune was telescopically discovered in September 1846 by astronomer Johann Gottfried Galle.
Neptune's existence and position were mathematically predicted prior to visual discovery due to irregularities in the orbit of Uranus.
French mathematician Urbain Le Verrier calculated the position of the unknown planet and sent his predictions to Galle at the Berlin Observatory.
Galle located Neptune on his first night of searching using Le Verrier's predicted coordinates.
Neptune is the only planet in the Solar System that cannot be seen with the naked human eye.
Neptune orbits at an average distance of about 30 astronomical units (roughly 2.8 billion miles or 4.5 billion kilometres) from the Sun.
Neptune's diameter is roughly four times that of Earth.
Galileo Galilei observed Neptune in 1612 and 1613, but mistook it for a fixed star.
William Lassell discovered Neptune's largest moon, Triton, just 17 days after Neptune itself was discovered.
Triton orbits Neptune in a retrograde direction, opposite to the planet's rotation.
NASA's Voyager 2 spacecraft flew by Neptune in 1989 and remains the only spacecraft to have visited the planet.
Neptune has the fastest planetary winds in the Solar System, reaching speeds of over 2,000 kilometres per hour (around 1,200 to 1,300 miles per hour).
Neptune rotates once on its axis in approximately 16 hours.
Methane in Neptune's atmosphere absorbs red light, contributing to the planet's blue coloration.
Neptune's axial tilt is approximately 28 degrees, causing seasonal cycles where each of the four seasons lasts around 40 Earth years.

disputed: Co-discovery credit between Le Verrier and British mathematician John Couch Adams: British astronomers claimed Adams predicted the planet independently, but historians have re-evaluated the 'Neptune papers' and questioned Adams's accuracy and culpability. The script should attribute the discovery directly to Le Verrier's sent coordinates, noting Adams's parallel British claim as contested.
Exact date of discovery: Sources S1, S2, and S7 cite September 23, 1846, while S5 cites the early hours of September 24, 1846. The script should use 'the night of September 23–24, 1846'.

Precise 2011 anniversary date: Source S1 notes the barycentric orbit completed on July 11, 2011, while the heliocentric position was reached on July 12, 2011. The script should generalize to 'July 2011' or state 'July 11 to 12, 2011, depending on the coordinate frame'.
